title: "I have told you. Now do as you choose." (18.59–18.66)
hook: after seven hundred verses, Krishna hands the decision back to Arjuna
tomorrow: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmabhuta: the whole road to Brahman in ten verses, and love at the summit. Your line was steady. Today, the most surprising move in the book.

Imagine the best teacher you ever had, spending months with you. Every question answered, every doubt heard, and once, a vision that nearly knocked you over. Then, at the very end, instead of saying, now you must do this, they close the book: I've told you everything. Think it over. Then do what you choose. That's chapter eighteen. God, in the Gita's own story, doesn't command the final move. He hands it back.
screen: `MONTHS OF ANSWERS.` → `ONE OVERWHELMING VISION.` → `THEN: DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning. Verse fifty-nine: if, leaning on your ego, you think, I will not fight, that decision is useless. Your own nature will push you to it. Verse sixty: bound by your own work, born of your nature, you'll do helplessly what you, confused, don't want to do. Then verse sixty-one, a strange picture: the Lord lives in the heart of every being, Arjuna, and by his power moves them all, as if they were mounted on a machine. Verse sixty-two: go to him for refuge with your whole being; by his grace you'll reach the highest peace. Then verse sixty-three. I have told you this wisdom, more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully. Then do as you wish. Yathecchasi tatha kuru. As you wish, so do. After all the teaching, all the argument, the vision of chapter eleven, Krishna doesn't force a choice. Many readers, especially modern teachers, find this one of the most striking moments in the book. The Gita's God persuades, shows, loves, and then respects Arjuna enough to let him decide. But he doesn't walk away. Verse sixty-four: hear my highest word once more. You are deeply loved by me. Verse sixty-five repeats a line from chapter nine: keep your mind on me, be devoted to me, and you will come to me. I promise you truly, for you are dear to me. So the handing back isn't cold. It comes wrapped in the plainest statement of love in the whole book. And it closes the week: sat, relinquishment, five causes, three kinds, your own dharma, steady, and now this.
screen: `YOUR NATURE WILL MOVE YOU.` · `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART.` · `REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU WISH.` · `YOU ARE DEEPLY LOVED.` · then, large: `NOW DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice you're facing, and let all the advice you've been given about it, from people, from books, from these days, be said once; then let it go quiet. In the quiet, reflect on it fully, the way verse sixty-three asks. You don't have to decide; just notice that the choice is yours, and that you can make it without fear.
Yathecchasi, as you wish. Gita eighteen, sixty-three: after all the teaching, Krishna says reflect fully, then do as you wish, yathecchasi tatha kuru.
Your line: he hands it back. He teaches fully, then trusts Arjuna with the choice. That's day two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often point to Gita 18.63, 'reflect fully, then do as you wish', as a sign that the Gita invites understanding and free choice rather than blind obedience.

chat.says: At the end of the Gita, does Krishna just order Arjuna what to do?
options: No. He teaches everything, then says reflect fully and do as you choose.
Yes. His very last word is a strict command to fight, no questions.
No. He gives up on Arjuna and leaves him to sort it out alone.
chat.meaning: In verse sixty-three Krishna says reflect fully, then do as you wish. Right after, he tells Arjuna he is deeply loved.

Yathecchasi.meaning: as you wish: Krishna's words handing Arjuna the choice
